source.title: RoFL: Attestable Robustness for Secure Federated Learning
source.authors: Hidde Lycklama; Lukas Burkhalter; Alexander Viand; Nicolas Küchler; Anwar Hithnawi

record.file_problem: The supplied full text is present; some PDF text and equations are flattened, but the relevant result sections are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports experiments on federated-learning backdoor persistence and defenses, including results it interprets through model memorization of rare tail examples. This is a new setting relative to the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper's architecture, optimizer, batch-size, regularization, width, and sharpness discussions are not its own tests of the listed versions. Its own experiments test the effect of removing memorized training examples only indirectly: the reported results concern backdoor attacks, norm bounds, and target subpopulations, not removal and retraining of influential memorized examples. Those results do not directly test any listed version. The paper cites the long-tail memorization finding from prior work; citations are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study investigates deliberately induced federated backdoors and secure aggregation, not any V1–V8 comparison. It invokes prior memorization findings to explain tail-backdoor persistence. Gaussian-noise memorization is not V1's fixed-random-label experiment, and no influential-example removal and retraining tests V8. A new setting alone does not establish T3.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. The authors conclude that suitable norm bounds substantially reduce practical FL attack risks, especially single-shot model replacement, but continuous attacks on tail targets remain possible. They interpret this vulnerability through models' capacity to memorize rare examples; they do not directly establish that such memorization is necessary for generalization.
record.recipe_differences: Federated-learning poisoning and secure-aggregation experiments; the paper studies backdoor behavior under norm-bounded client updates rather than the centralized natural-label generalization or memorization-removal recipes in the versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Target subpopulation (prototypical versus tail), attack duration (single-shot versus continuous), norm-bound size and selection, and fraction of compromised clients change attack persistence or success.

fits_no_version.finding: Without norm bounds, single-shot tail backdoors persist longer than prototypical backdoors; Gaussian-noise targets can also remain memorized. Appropriate norm bounds prevent the tested single-shot injections.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Deliberately implanted federated backdoors persist longer on rare target inputs than on prototypical inputs.

fits_no_version.finding: Under median-based norm bounds, continuous tail attacks reach 50% backdoor accuracy after 75 rounds for FMN and 500 for C10, while prototypical attacks stay below 10%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Repeated malicious participation can implant tail backdoors despite norm bounds that suppress prototypical backdoors.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
record.problems: The relevant attack results are presented mainly in figures, and the experiments concern federated backdoor attacks rather than the generalization measures in the listed versions. No uncertainty estimates are reported for these attack outcomes in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying rows for the listed versions: the paper does not report results from those version-specific interventions or measurements. Its attack-accuracy plots and norm-bound experiments concern federated poisoning behavior, which none of V1–V8 measures; the text also cites prior memorization work rather than testing example removal.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting versus natural-label generalization under the same architecture and training recipe, including chance-level held-out performance on random labels.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects on held-out error and interactions with dataset size, augmentation, or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness rankings of generalization gaps versus other measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples, followed by retraining and test-accuracy measurement.

record.verdict_notes: The empty result-row set is appropriate for V1–V8. Sections 2.4–2.5 discuss memorization, but their attack results do not test the versions' specified interventions or comparisons. Update norm bounds are also distinct from V7's magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation sharpness.

versions.untested_parts: No fixed-random-label versus natural-label training comparison or held-out accuracy comparison.
No width sweep past interpolation or test-error measurement across widths.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No adaptive versus SGD optimizer comparison on held-out performance.
No large-batch versus small-batch generalization comparison.
No dropout or weight-decay ablation for held-out error.
No sharpness or other generalization-measure comparison.
No removal of memorized training examples followed by retraining and test-accuracy measurement.
